t.3.57.2: Then, O king, the daughter of Bhīma, overcome with fear and grief, pondered that very great task concerning the king.
t.3.57.1: Then Damayantī, seeing the lord of men of holy renown, his mind lost in gambling, acting like a madman though not mad,
t.3.57.4: Bṛhatsenā, go and summon the ministers by Nala's command, and tell them what wealth has been taken away and what treasure remains.
t.3.57.3: Fearing that calamity and wishing to do what was dear to him, and perceiving that Nala had been stripped of all his possessions, she spoke these words.
t.3.57.5: Then all those ministers, learning Nala's command, said, "Perhaps such is our lot," and went back again.
t.3.57.7: Seeing that her husband did not welcome her words, Damayantī, ashamed, went back into the house.
t.3.57.6: All those subjects had gathered there a second time, and Bhīma's daughter informed him of it, but he did not welcome it.
t.3.57.8: Perceiving that the dice were constantly turned against Puṇyaśloka, and that Nala had been robbed of all his possessions, she spoke again to her nurse.
t.3.57.9: Bṛhatsenā, go once more and, at Nala's command, bring the charioteer Vārṣṇeya, O fair lady; a great task is at hand.
t.3.57.10: Bṛhatsenā, having heard those words spoken by Damayantī, had Vārṣṇeya brought by trusted men who carried out commands faithfully.
t.3.57.11: Then Bhaimī, the blameless one who knew the right place and time, soothing Vārṣṇeya with gentle words, spoke to him what the moment called for.
t.3.57.13: For the more the king is defeated here by Puṣkara, the more his passion for the dice grows ever greater.
t.3.57.12: You know how the king has always conducted himself rightly toward you. Now that he has fallen into distress, you ought to give him your help.
t.3.57.14: And just as Puṣkara's dice remain obedient to his will, so too is the reverse seen in Nala's dice.
t.3.57.16: Since the king, deluded, does not welcome my words, I have come to you for refuge, O charioteer; do as I say. For my heart finds no peace, fearing that he may at some point be ruined.
t.3.57.15: He does not properly heed the words of his friends and kinsmen; surely, I think, nothing remains to the great-souled Naiṣadha.
t.3.57.17: Yoke Nala's beloved horses of great speed, place this pair of children upon the chariot, and go to Kuṇḍina.
t.3.57.18: Leave the two children with my kinsmen, and the chariot as well, and these horses; then, as you please, either stay there or go elsewhere.
t.3.57.19: Then Vārṣṇeya, Nala's charioteer, reported those words of Damayantī in full to Nala's ministers, to the chief among them first.
t.3.57.21: Having left there the horses and that excellent chariot, the charioteer also left the girl Indrasenā and the boy Indrasena.
t.3.57.22: Having taken leave of King Bhīma, the charioteer, distressed and grieving for King Nala, wandered on and then went to the city of Ayodhyā.
t.3.57.20: Having met with them and come to a decision, he, with their leave, O lord of the earth, set the pair of children upon it and went to the Vidarbhas with that chariot.
t.3.57.23: Deeply grieved, he presented himself before King Ṛtuparṇa, and, O lord of the earth, he entered his service, earning his wages as a charioteer.
